# A complete geometric family: higher-spin stabilizers generated by individual twists

**Problem:** TOP-2754

**Claim type:** Literature report

**Exact scope:** For closed genus g≥5 and r dividing 2g−2, higher-spin stabilizers give finite-index subgroups generated by individual Dehn twists. Their indices and conjugacy classes for fixed r are classified by parity/Arf invariant. This is a complete classification within this natural family, not of all twist-generated finite-index subgroups.

For every \(g\geq5\) and positive divisor \(r\mid2g-2\), let \(\phi\) be an \(r\)-spin structure on the closed oriented surface. One convenient definition is the \(\mathbb Z/r\)-valued winding-number function on oriented simple curves used by Calderon–Salter: it satisfies twist-linearity and homological coherence, and a small positively oriented disk boundary has value \(1\). Define
\[
 \operatorname{Mod}_g[\phi]=\{f:f\cdot\phi=\phi\}.
\]
These are stabilizers of genuine tangent-bundle/geometric data, rather than stabilizers invented from an arbitrary coset action.

The checked published theorem proves that each such subgroup is generated by twists about \(\phi\)-admissible nonseparating curves, meaning \(\phi(c)=0\). This is the equality of the admissible subgroup with the full stabilizer in Proposition 5.1. Theorem C strengthens it to explicit finite configurations of twist generators. Merely proving that each admissible twist preserves \(\phi\) would give only one containment; the reverse containment is the substantial theorem.

Here is the exact enumeration within this family. For fixed \(r\), the mapping class group has one orbit on spin structures if \(r\) is odd, and two if \(r\) is even, distinguished by \(\operatorname{Arf}(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\). Stabilizers in an orbit are conjugate. Their indices are
\[
 [\operatorname{Mod}_g:\operatorname{Mod}_g[\phi]]
 =\begin{cases}
 r^{2g},&r\text{ odd},\\
 (r/2)^{2g}2^{g-1}(2^g+1),&r\text{ even},\ \operatorname{Arf}=0,\\
 (r/2)^{2g}2^{g-1}(2^g-1),&r\text{ even},\ \operatorname{Arf}=1 .
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{1}
\]
In the even case the indices differ, so the two stabilizers cannot be conjugate. The family thus has exactly one or two conjugacy classes for each specified \(r\).

The count can be understood from the source's affine coordinates. An \(r\)-spin structure is uniquely determined by arbitrary values on a geometric homology basis, giving \(r^{2g}\) structures. For even \(r\), reduction modulo two has \((r/2)^{2g}\) lifts over each quadratic refinement. In symplectic coordinates, a refinement is specified by \(g\) pairs \((a_i,b_i)\in\mathbb F_2^2\), with Arf invariant \(\sum_i a_i b_i\). There are three even pairs and one odd pair, so the even-minus-odd count is \(2^g\), while the total is \(4^g\). Solving gives \(2^{g-1}(2^g\pm1)\), yielding (1).

For \(r=2\), the associated quadratic form uses \(q([c])=\phi(c)+1\); confusing these conventions reverses the admissible-twist test. The classification here already satisfies the strongest of the listed generation restrictions, individual twists. It provides no converse saying every twist-generated finite-index subgroup must preserve one spin structure, nor does it classify groups generated only by multitwists or powers. Those broader classification requests remain beyond the checked family theorem.

References actually checked:

- A. Calderon and N. Salter, Higher spin mapping class groups and strata of Abelian differentials over Teichmüller space, Adv. Math. 389 (2021), Article 107926; arXiv:1906.03515v2, 29 June 2021, Theorem C, Definitions 2.1, 2.7, Lemmas 2.4 and 2.15, Proposition 5.1 and Section 6. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.03515
